The inclusion of iron compounds in maize flour or cornmeal at low consumption levels depends on the sensory characteristics of the final product, which must be tested for feasibility at an industrial scale. 2. High-extraction flour, also referred to as whole flour, retains significant levels of natural maize phytates. These phytates inhibit the absorption of iron and zinc in the human body. 3. Nixtamalization is a process used to produce high-extraction maize flour, whereas degermination and precooking result in low-extraction flour. 4. The daily consumption of maize flour and cornmeal varies significantly across countries, ranging from approximately 50 grams per person in Ghana, Haiti, and Uganda to 300 grams per person in Lesotho and Malawi. 5. When the estimated per capita consumption of maize flour is less than 75 grams per day, it becomes challenging to add sufficient fortificants to meet the micronutrient needs of women of childbearing age. In such cases, additional food fortification vehicles and other interventions may need to be considered. 6. The amounts of iron mentioned are expressed in milligrams of elemental iron. The specific quantity of an iron compound to be added should be calculated based on the molecular weight of the compound. 7. Both zinc sulfate and zinc oxide can be used for maize fortification, although zinc oxide is more cost-effective. However, the bioavailability of zinc is influenced by the concentration of phytates, which is higher in flours with high extraction rates. 8. Zinc fortification levels assume a dietary intake of 5 mg of zinc and no additional phytate intake from other dietary sources. 9. Vitamin B12 deficiency is highly prevalent across all age groups, reaching up to 50% in some countries. It is recommended to include vitamin B12 when fortifying flour with folic acid. 10. Restoring certain B-complex vitamins should be a standard practice in all settings, particularly in nixtamalized maize flour. 11. Evaluating the efficacy and effectiveness of maize flour and cornmeal fortification programs, either alone or in combination with wheat flour fortification, is essential for all age groups. 12. Determining appropriate levels and combinations of nutrients, their interactions, the stability of micronutrient compounds, and their acceptability to consumers is critical. 13. Biomarkers of individual micronutrient status should be assessed under varying conditions of infection and inflammation. 14. The impact of maize use for biofuel production on food security and the sustainability of maize flour and cornmeal fortification programs should be analyzed. 15. The feasibility of small-scale fortification of maize flour and cornmeal for public health programs should be explored. 16. Dissemination of guidelines will occur through electronic media, including slide presentations, the WHO Nutrition website, social media, and the e-Library of Evidence for Nutrition Actions (eLENA). These platforms compile WHO guidelines, systematic reviews, and evidence that informed the recommendations. 17. The guidelines will also be shared through a network of international partners, including WHO offices, ministries of health, collaborating centers, universities, UN agencies, and NGOs. 18. Derivative products, such as summaries and compilations of recommendations related to food fortification, may be developed to aid end-users. 19. Efforts will be made to improve access to these guidelines for stakeholders facing barriers to information or those crucial to implementing the recommendations, such as policymakers and subnational decision-makers. 20. Disseminated information should emphasize the benefits of food fortification programs in regions where micronutrient deficiencies are a public health concern, particularly in rural or isolated areas with limited access to fortified foods. 21. The guideline provides evidence-based recommendations to member states on the effects and safety of fortifying maize flour and cornmeal with micronutrients. This strategy aims to improve population health, prevent iron deficiency, and reduce the risk of neural tube defects. 22. Member states adopting these recommendations should conduct thorough assessments of policy implications and align the fortification strategy with their national plans for preventing and controlling micronutrient deficiencies. 23. A robust baseline database on the prevalence of micronutrient deficiencies across populations is essential for program planning and monitoring. 24. Data should be disaggregated to identify health inequities across population groups, such as age, disability, migration status, and political environment. 25. WHO has developed tools like the Health Equity Assessment Toolkit (HEAT) to assist member states in assessing health inequalities and adapting the guidelines to their contexts. 26. Fortification programs should be culturally appropriate to ensure acceptance, adoption, and sustainability. Resistance based on social beliefs or established practices should be identified and addressed. 27. Accurate and evidence-based information about fortified maize flour should be disseminated to prevent misconceptions, particularly in low-resource settings and among populations with low education levels. 28. Local leaders and culturally relevant communication strategies should be employed to improve the acceptability and adoption of fortified maize products. 29. Programs should have clear objectives that consider available resources, existing policies, delivery platforms, communication channels, and potential stakeholders. 30. Fortification programs should be part of a coordinated and comprehensive strategy to address micronutrient deficiencies, potentially including multiple food items. 31. National programs should account for coexisting mass-fortification initiatives and adjust micronutrient levels accordingly. 32. Fortification programs for maize flour and cornmeal with iron and folic acid should be coordinated with antenatal care programs that supplement pregnant women with these nutrients. 33. In malaria-endemic settings, women may receive folic acid through fortified foods or supplements to prevent neural tube defects, alongside antimalarial medications. 34. Recent evidence suggests that folate supplementation does not reduce the efficacy of antifolate malaria treatments when doses are appropriate for preventing neural tube defects. 35. Communication strategies should be culturally appropriate and tailored to the target populations to ensure the intervention is understood and its benefits are recognized. 36. Concurrent measures, such as awareness campaigns, food subsidies, and direct distribution of fortified flours, can help mitigate health inequities caused by differential access to fortified foods.
